title: White Citizens Council, Eisenhower tickets and an integrated political group
summary: He tells of the DA affair, being refused entry at an Eisenhower event, and forming a New Orleans political association with Earl Amadee and others.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: Well, what were they going to charge you with? I mean, what could they have?

Well, I don't know what he was charging me, but they, but a certain, certain whites and I got, got it in black and white. I got letters and I have cards that were sent to me by the white citizen council. And, uh, incidentally, uh, prior to that, I was a registered Republican incidentally, and I was on a Republican committee, uh, when, uh, when, uh, um, Eisenhower was running for office. And I sold somewhere around about, uh, a few hundred dollars worth of tickets. They wouldn't even let me go into the front door to attend the affair when Eisenhower came to New Orleans at Fairmount Hotel. Today I can walk in the door and incidentally today, I also handled some of the advertising for the Fairmount Hotel as the account executive for the Fairmount. I did it for a while. And, uh, so things were beginning to change. And, uh, I, I'll say great day for the city of New Orleans. There were some beautiful things were beginning to happen. And I guess I can tell some, uh, dynamic stories about people who, uh, accelerated, uh, the new ideology. Uh, in the city of New Orleans, Jackson V. A Cox, uh, the state representative Avery Alexander, Carl Gallman. Uh, maybe a lot of people may not like some of these names I'm calling, but these people, uh, they, they agitated the situation. Well, you know what an agitator is. You throw your clothes in the washing machine. An agitator with the soap will get the clean, will get your clothes clean. This is what agitator is all about. But it was a lot of fun. But, uh, they didn't lock me up when I went before Dallin. But, uh, Dallin and I, Mr. Dallin and I got to be very, very good friends. And, uh, Earl Amadee, myself, and the late, uh, uh, George, uh, uh, oh, he just died here recently. Boy, I'm just trying to think. Uh, Augustine. We were the first, we put together, uh, uh, uh, I think one of the first integrated political organizations in the city of New Orleans. Uh-huh. And that was in 1955, 56 or something like that. And we just traveled. We traveled the state. We, we were, uh, uh, I think we, at that time, Earl said we're going to support Russell Long. Uh, Earl Long, rather. Not Russell. It was, uh, Russell's nephew became state senator. But, uh, we supported him. And, uh, uh, we had a lot of fun traveling because, uh, uh, sometime we put our own money up. Sometime they would, they would sponsor us. But we mostly would put our, our own money up. And, and, and we, uh, uh, uh, would come along pretty good with this political structure.
Well, was there a name for the organization?

Uh, I'm trying to think of the name. It was called the New Orleans Political Association. I think, I think that's the name I remember. But we had another, another name. I, I think the name was changed somewhere in time. And, uh, I left town. I went over to Texas on a trip or something like that and stayed over there for a while. When I came back, the name was changed. But, uh, some of the same people were active. Some of the same people died into it. Then, along came, uh, Ernest Wright, uh, who was one of the founders of the People's Defense League uptown here, right across from Shakespeare Park.
